gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Apple TV 4K's own port is Gigabit Ethernet and that a gigabit NAS measured at 115 MB/s (920 Mbps) carries 7.2 times the 128 Mbps ceiling of a 100 GB Ultra HD Blu-ray. So any 2.5GbE or Intel box, such as the DXP2800 at $389.99 against the DH2300 at $239.99 on UGREEN's store today, costs $150 more for speed Infuse on an Apple TV can't use.
standout_why: Firecore's cited 'Streaming From a Mac, PC, or NAS' page gives no bitrate, network speed or hardware figure; it only covers SMB version settings. firecore.com/infuse is a product page with no NAS sizing. The top non-cited result, itechguides.com (prices dated 2026-11-17), lists the DH2300 ($239.99), DXP2800 ($379.99), DS225+ ($364.29) and AS1202T ($199.99) with vendor speed claims (125 MB/s, 282 MB/s, 2.5GbE), but it never compares them with a remux bitrate or with the Apple TV's 1GbE port, and it gives no running cost. ChatGPT's answer says 'Gigabit Ethernet' is enough, which is the right direction, but it gives no number for the margin and no yearly power cost.
decides: It confirms that the cheapest gigabit ARM box is the right pick and rules out paying more for 2.5GbE or Intel N100/J4125 models when the only goal is Infuse direct play. Gigabit has about 7× headroom over the highest UHD Blu-ray bitrate, and the Apple TV 4K can't go past 1 Gb/s anyway. Within that tier, running cost separates the 1-bay DS124 (about $17 a year at Synology's rated access power) from the 2-bay DS223j (about $26 a year), so the extra bay costs about $9 a year in electricity.
